newsitem.title: FRANCE: French politicians sceptical of EU jobs pact.
newsitem.headline: French politicians sceptical of EU jobs pact.

text.p: French politicians were sceptical on Tuesday over a European Union pledge at the Amsterdam summit to pay more attention to jobs and growth in the run-up to monetary union without providing more money for the task.

Conservative ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing said the EU leaders' pledge made to accommodate demands from France's new left-wing government "has little practical value since they said they would not put in an extra cent".

"It was not a success for France, but it was a success for Europe," he told LCI television, welcoming the confirmation in Amsterdam of the stability pact to maintain budgetary discipline after the launch of the planned single currency.

Opposition conservatives were split between those satisfied that the stability pact had been upheld and others who regretted that no funds had been set aside to boost growth and curb France's record 12.8 percent unemployment.
The Greens party, a member of Prime Minister Lionel Jospin's leftist coalition, said the accord was symbolic and vowed to keep pushing for "a social Europe that...remains to be built".

Communist Andre Lajoinie, also a member of the ruling coalition, said the agreement had failed to loosen the stranglehold imposed by the Maastricht Treaty on economic and monetary union. "It is up to the social movement to continue the work," he said.
Socialist Jack Lang, freshly elected head of the National Asembly's Foreign Affairs Committee, said the Amsterdam agreement was "a first step".
He said France on its own could not impose its will on its partners but had put a foot in a door that had been locked. "It is the start of a movement that will gather momentum," he said.
While left-wing newspapers offered cautious praise, right-wing and business dailies were critical of an agreement seen as largely symbolic and unable to immediately create jobs.
"A window was opened. Very good," the left-of-centre Liberation said. "(But) we are still far from the European growth pact envisioned by the Socialist Party congress."
The financial daily Les Echos called the last-minute compromise a "face-saving" gesture that allowed all parties to pull back from the brink of rejecting the stability pact.

France had won an expression of EU concern on jobs, the paper said, but had lost out on its other main demands -- to establish a "true economic government" to serve as a counterweight to the planned European central bank, and to launch new major infrastructure projects to reduce unemployment.
It said a European jobs summit in October would test whether Britain, Germany and French could jointly commmit to anything more than vague objectives. "To tell the truth, there is little chance."
The right-wing daily Le Figaro said France, and Europe, had "scored a point", but Jospin's reliance on the state and the EU to "restart the job creation machine" was misplaced.
"With these solutions, we do not see why he would succeed better than the previous government," it said.
The Communist daily l'Humanite portrayed the jobs and growth resolution put forward by the Jospin government as marking a new stage in the battle against joblessness.

"In fact, a ghost is haunting Europe -- the ghost of unemployment. For the first time it has also haunted the highest circles of diplomacy, disturbing the well-oiled European clockwork...(and) inspiring the drafting of this new text. A new social and political realm is opening in the battle for jobs."
